--- title: "Bayesian *t*-Tests and Diagnostics" subtitle: "PSYC 6019-A01 / PSYC 6022-A01
2025-10-09 | Lab 7" author: "Jess Helmer" footer: "[jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/)" format: revealjs: code-link: true slide-number: true code-line-numbers: false theme: ../../gt-theme.scss width: 1200 execute: echo: true dpi: 600 freeze: auto knitr: opts_chunk: dev: svg --- ## Outline - Bayesian *t*-tests - Diagnostics ::: {.cell} ::: # Bayesian *t*-Tests ## Bayesian *t*-Tests A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `rstanarm` R package! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("rstanarm") library(rstanarm) filtered_mpg <- mpg |> filter(when_any(cyl == 4, cyl == 8)) ``` :::
:::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} freq_t_test <- t.test(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg) freq_t_test ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch Two Sample t-test data: hwy by cyl t = 17.586, df = 144.65, p-value < 2.2e-16 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 4 and group 8 is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 9.918065 12.429731 sample estimates: mean in group 4 mean in group 8 28.80247 17.62857 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, family = "gaussian") summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 10% 50% 90% (Intercept) 40.0 1.0 38.7 40.0 41.2 cyl -2.8 0.2 -3.0 -2.8 -2.6 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.7 4.0 4.3 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 10% 50% 90% mean_PPD 23.6 0.5 23.0 23.6 24.2 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 3618 cyl 0.0 1.0 3713 sigma 0.0 1.0 3739 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 3861 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1719 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Priors for model 'bayes_t_test' ------ Intercept (after predictors centered) Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 17) Coefficients Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 8.6) Auxiliary (sigma) Specified prior: ~ exponential(rate = 1) Adjusted prior: ~ exponential(rate = 0.15) ------ See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details ``` ::: ::: ## Model $$ \begin{aligned} \text{highway MPG}_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{cylinders}_i + \epsilon_i && \text{likelihood: a linear model} \\ \beta_0 &\sim N(24, 17) && \text{prior for intercept} \\ \beta_1 &\sim N(0, 8.6) && \text{prior for slope} \\ \epsilon &\sim \text{Exponential}(0.15) && \text{prior for residual variance} \end{aligned} $$ ## Credible Intervals :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Equal Tailed Interval** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} posterior_interval(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 5% 95% (Intercept) 38.337565 41.592614 cyl -3.057753 -2.526213 sigma 3.645302 4.417041 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Highest Density Interval** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("bayestestR") bayestestR::hdi(bayes_t_test, component = "all") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Highest Density Interval Parameter | 95% HDI ---------------------------- (Intercept) | [37.99, 41.93] cyl | [-3.12, -2.49] # Fixed effects (sigma) Parameter | 95% HDI -------------------------- sigma | [ 3.57, 4.48] ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: # Diagnostics ## Diagnostics with Bayes Most of the time, Bayes' theorem $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)}$ is too complex to solve analytically. So, we estimate Bayesian models with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The job of MCMC is to explore and sample from the posterior probability distribution $P(\theta | D)$ for all $\theta$ at a rate proportional to each probability. So, after many MCMC samples, we end up with a density distribution of samples with height matching $P(\theta | D)$, and we can use those samples to make inferences about our parameters and outcomes! ::: subpoint ○ E.g., we believe there is a 90% chance the difference in highway MPG between four- and eight-cylinder cars is within the interval [-3.06, -2.53]. ::: But, all this hinges on the MCMC sampler---we have to check it for evidence that it *sampled well*. ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scale_colors <- c("steelblue", "#D98282", "#6BAE9D", "#8C7AAE") x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.svg){width=576} ::: ::: ::: [This is called a *trace plot*. It shows the samplers' samples for each iteration it runs. Can you tell if this sampler sampled well?]{.fragment} ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 2, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.svg){width=576} ::: ::: [What if I told you we ran another, completely separate run, and its samples looked like this?]{.fragment} ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 3, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.svg){width=576} ::: ::: [Or a third?]{.fragment} ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 4, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.svg){width=576} ::: ::: [A fourth? How much confidence do you have in the sampler now?]{.fragment} [They cannot guarantee the sampler is **correctly** sampling from the distribution, but if we run multiple *chains* (separate runs of MCMC, each doing their own thing independently), we can at least check if the sampler is sampling **consistently**.]{.fragment} ## House Layout Example ## Looking at the Samples Our example's trace plots! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("bayesplot") library(bayesplot) mcmc_trace(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.svg){width=1152} ::: ::: [Good! They look like "fuzzy caterpillars".]{.fragment} ## Trace Rank Plots These are called "trace rank" plots. They're very similar to trace plots, except they *order* the samples in magnitude. It's mostly personal preference, but these are sometimes easier to see bad chains. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mcmc_rank_overlay(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.svg){width=960} ::: ::: [What does a bad chain look like?]{.fragment} ## Bad Sampling Example Messing with the algorithm on purpose to make it sample poorly... ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'continuous' NOW (CHAIN 1). Rhat ($\hat{R}$, read "R-hat") is a measure of convergence among different MCMC *chains*. The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.svg){width=960} ::: ::: ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.svg){width=960} ::: ::: ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.svg){width=960} ::: ::: Variance between chain means is sooo different from variance within chains! ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.svg){width=960} ::: ::: ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.svg){width=960} ::: ::: ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.svg){width=960} ::: ::: Variance between chain means is very close to variance within chains! ## Rhat In practice, you want to see $\hat{R}$ values less than 1.01. ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test)[, "Rhat"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) cyl sigma mean_PPD log-posterior 0.9998327 1.0001064 0.9995895 0.9998624 1.0006671 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Effective Sample Size (ESS) In order to closely approximate the posterior ($P(\theta | D)$, the point of this all!), we need to make sure we have a large number of MCMC samples. ## Lab 07 Assignment

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
